steps.title: When the antecedent is the object
body: Every relative clause you've built so far had the antecedent doing the action: الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي سَافَرَ, "the man who traveled." But what about الْكِتَابُ الَّذِي قَرَأْتُهُ, "the book that I read"? Here الْكِتَابُ isn't doing the reading — it's what gets read. Arabic can't just say قَرَأْتُ ("I read") and leave it at that; the verb needs a resumptive pronoun pointing back at the antecedent: قَرَأْتُهُ, "I read it." It's the exact same attached-pronoun suffix you already know from gr:attached-possessive and from إنّ's family — just landing on a verb this time instead of a noun or a particle.

الْمَرْأَةُ الَّتِي رَأَيْتُهَا سَعِيدَةٌ ("the woman that I saw is happy") does the same thing with ـهَا. Drop the resumptive pronoun and the sentence is simply incomplete — رَأَيْتُ alone doesn't say who or what was seen.

Separately: الَّذِي and الَّتِي are strictly singular. A group of people needs its own relative pronoun — الَّذِينَ for masculine plural, اللَّاتِي for feminine plural: الْمُعَلِّمُونَ الَّذِينَ فِي الْمَدْرَسَةِ مَشْغُولُونَ ("the teachers who are at school are busy"). A non-human plural still takes singular الَّتِي, unchanged from what you already know about plural agreement — الَّذِينَ/اللَّاتِي are specifically for people.

steps.title: Four sentences, two new ideas
steps.intro: Read each sentence and find either the resumptive pronoun on the verb, or the plural relative pronoun. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: The missing piece
steps.prompt: What job does the ـهُ on قَرَأْتُهُ do?

options.label: It points back at الْكِتَابُ — "I read it"
It marks the verb as past tense
It's decorative and could be dropped

steps.explanation: الْكِتَابُ is the OBJECT of قَرَأْتُ, not its subject, so the verb needs a resumptive pronoun (ـهُ) to stand in for it — without it, the sentence would be incomplete.

steps.title: A familiar suffix, a new host
steps.prompt: Where else have you seen a suffix like ـهَا do a similar resuming job?

options.label: Nowhere — this is a brand new kind of suffix

steps.explanation: The same attached-pronoun suffixes you met on nouns (gr:attached-possessive) and on إنّ's family (أَنَّهَا) now resume an object-relative clause's antecedent on a verb — one mechanic, three different hosts.

steps.title: More than one person
steps.prompt: Why الَّذِينَ here instead of الَّذِي?

options.label: الْمُعَلِّمُونَ is a plural, human antecedent — الَّذِينَ is required for that, not the singular الَّذِي
الَّذِينَ and الَّذِي are interchangeable in every context
الَّذِينَ is only used for non-human antecedents

steps.explanation: الَّذِي/الَّتِي are strictly singular. A plural group of people takes الَّذِينَ (masculine) or اللَّاتِي (feminine) instead — never الَّذِي repeated.

steps.title: The feminine plural counterpart
steps.prompt: الْمُعَلِّمَاتُ is the sound feminine plural of مُعَلِّمَة. Which relative pronoun must match it?

options.label: اللَّاتِي — the feminine plural relative pronoun
الَّتِي — the feminine singular relative pronoun
الَّذِينَ — the masculine plural relative pronoun

steps.explanation: اللَّاتِي is الَّتِي's plural counterpart, exactly the way الَّذِينَ is to الَّذِي — both agree with a plural, human antecedent's gender and number together.

steps.title: Relative clauses, completed
steps.message: Subject- and object-relative, singular and plural — the full working set for describing people and things with a clause. Dual relative pronouns and joining ideas into paragraphs are still ahead for this unit.
